events.objective: Establish the true symptom onset and blast radius from metrics only (auth-service logs unavailable). Determine: (1) exact time the 401/invalid_token rate first rose from baseline (minute-level, using auth-service request/error/latency metrics and any 401 series); (2) whether the 36% error rate is stable, plateaued, or stepping up in discrete jumps (suggesting partial rollout vs. global break); (3) which OTHER services across the fleet show 401s, error-rate spikes, or latency changes since that onset — especially services in the identity namespace and any API gateway/edge — to test whether this is auth-only or broader; (4) whether auth-service resource metrics (CPU, memory, restarts, instance count, saturation) changed around onset; (5) whether there is any evidence of clock skew or a drop in an outbound key-fetch/JWKS dependency metric. Report concrete series names, values, and timestamps.

Build the change and dependency picture for the incident window without relying on auth-service logs. Determine: (1) all deployments and config changes (across ALL services/namespaces, not just auth-service) between ~2026-04-15T06:00Z and now, with exact times, targets, and diff summaries; (2) auth-service's upstream/downstream dependency graph — who issues tokens, who validates them, what shared components exist (JWKS/key service, identity DB, cache, config/secrets store, ingress), and which of those live in the identity namespace; (3) any change to secrets/certs/key-rotation or TTL settings in that window; (4) whether any deployment/config change plausibly touched only a subset of instances (canary/rolling/partial). Return a ranked list of candidate changes with timestamps.

Correlate and disambiguate: take the onset time from task a and the candidate change/dependency list from task b and rank which change (if any) actually precedes and aligns with the onset, distinguishing a partial/canary rollout from a full one. Then search historical incidents for (i) prior invalid_token / 401 mass-logout events, (ii) prior incidents where a log-pipeline outage in one namespace masked or coincided with a real fault, and (iii) key-rotation or JWKS staleness precedents. Deliver the top hypothesis with supporting/contradicting evidence and a specific falsification test (e.g., 'if X change was rolled back at T and 401s persisted, hypothesis is dead').

events.statement: Across ALL services, exactly 2 deployments occurred in the window 2026-04-15T05:00Z–16:00Z: market-data-service v5.0.3 at 11:35:00Z ('Fix symbol mapping', ci-bot) and auth-service v7.3.0 at 14:00:00Z ('Upgrade JWT library to 4.x; refactor token validation', d.verma). The auth-service deploy is the one temporally aligned with onset (~14:12Z report).

auth-service v7.3.0 explicitly rewrote token validation with a breaking library change: changes listed as 'jjwt 0.11 -> 0.12 (breaking parser API)' and 'TokenValidator rewritten'. No rollback recorded (rolled_back_at: null).

Exactly 1 config change occurred in the window (all services scope): auth-service key 'jwt.signing.key_id' changed 2026-04-15T14:01:00Z from 'k-2025-10' to 'k-2026-04', author security-automation, description 'Scheduled signing-key rotation' — one minute after the v7.3.0 deploy.

auth-service dependency graph (depth 2): caller api-gateway -> auth-service (http); auth-service -> user-db (postgres, db), redis-cache (cache, SHARED=true), kyc-provider (external, no telemetry). No JWKS endpoint, key-service, or secrets-store node appears in the graph; redis-cache is the only shared component auth-service attaches to, and user-db is flagged shared=false.

Only auth-service is owned by namespace/owner 'identity' in the retrieved dependency data; its dependencies (user-db, redis-cache, api-gateway) are owned by 'platform'/'edge'. So the identity namespace contains auth-service, while its datastore/cache neighbours do not — meaning an identity-namespace log outage would cover auth-service logs only.

redis-cache is a shared component with 4 consumer edges (auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) plus downstream callers, so a cache-side degradation could affect auth-service and others simultaneously. Redis-cache neighbor data shows no direct deployment/config change attributed to it in the window.

events.answer: Two changes landed within ~2 minutes of each other at the incident onset: auth-service deploy v7.3.0 at 14:00:00Z (JWT library jjwt 0.11->0.12 breaking parser API, TokenValidator rewritten) and a scheduled JWT signing-key rotation (jwt.signing.key_id k-2025-10 -> k-2026-04) at 14:01:00Z. Neither candidate change was rolled back or superseded during the plateau: querying deployments 14:01–15:59Z (all services) returns count 0, and querying config changes 14:01–15:59Z returns only the same cfg-2705 record at 14:01:00Z. Precedent for the deployment path: HIST-109 (2025-07-11, auth-service) 'Token validation regression after auth library upgrade', symptoms '401 invalid_token'/'token validation failures', root_cause 'JWT library upgrade changed clock-skew default', category 'bad_deployment', resolution 'Rolled back; pinned skew config', match_score 4 in the invalid_token search — i.e. the same class of change (auth library upgrade) has previously caused an identical symptom via a config default (clock skew), not necessarily a full parser failure.

Sufficient evidence to distinguish a partial/canary rollout from a full one is NOT available: the deployment record carries no rollout strategy or instance/percentage field, and the only graph shared component on auth-service's path is redis-cache (SHARED, 4 consumer edges) with no deployment/config change attributed to it — so nothing in the retrieved data shows what fraction of auth-service instances took v7.3.0 or k-2026-04.

No historical precedent exists in the incident store for a log-pipeline/telemetry outage masking or coinciding with a real fault: the namespace-outage search returned only two unrelated dependency-failure cases (HIST-103 exchange partner outage, HIST-105 bank partner API outage) and no incident whose root cause involves missing logs concealing a fault.

events.answer: Ranking by (a) temporal precedence of onset and (b) alignment: the JWT signing-key rotation (jwt.signing.key_id k-2025-10 -> k-2026-04, 14:01Z, cfg-2705) is ranked #1 because onset (14:02:00) is exactly one minute after it and it is the same failure mode as precedent HIST-108 ("Key rotation published new key id before all pods loaded the JWKS"); the auth-service v7.3.0 deploy (14:00Z, dep-5710, breaking jjwt 0.11->0.12 parser rewrite) is ranked #2 — it precedes onset by 2 minutes and is a one-shot rewrite, so if it were a deterministic parser bug the plateau would be either 100% (global break) or a step matching new-instance traffic share, not a flat 36%. Neither candidate has any recorded rollback or any second change during the 14:02–15:59 plateau, so the data cannot yet separate them; the discriminating facts (per-instance version/key_id, traffic split across pods) are not exposed. The key distinction is real, not canary-vs-full: the plateau is a single discrete cliff (0.16% -> 36.08% within 60s) that never steps again, which fits a subset of pods/validators holding a stale or incompatible key/library state rather than a full-fleet break (full break would be ~100%). Falsification tests: (1) if the 401 rate is decomposed and is uniform across ALL auth-service instances/versions, the partial-state hypothesis dies; (2) if k-2026-04 was reverted (or JWKS old key re-published) and 401s persisted at 36%, the key-rotation hypothesis dies and the v7.3.0 rewrite takes #1; (3) if reverting dep-5710 (keeping the new key) does not reduce 401s, HIST-109-style library regression is dead; (4) if a non-auth caller of the JWKS/key path, or api-gateway itself, shows matching 401s, that proves a shared key/JWKS fault rather than auth-service-internal code. Precedents: invalid_token/401 mass-logout = HIST-109 and HIST-108; key-rotation/JWKS staleness = HIST-108 (re-published previous key; staged rotation). Searches for "log-pipeline outage masking a real fault" returned NO matching incident — only two unrelated dependency-failure cases (HIST-103, HIST-105), so there is no repository precedent for log-absence masking a fault.

Determine: (1) all deployments and config changes (across ALL services/namespaces, not just auth-service) between ~2026-04-15T06:00Z and now, with exact times, targets, and diff summaries; (2) auth-service's upstream/downstream dependency graph — who issues tokens, who validates them, what shared components exist (JWKS/key service, identity DB, cache, config/secrets store, ingress), and which of those live in the identity namespace; (3) any change to secrets/certs/key-rotation or TTL settings in that window; (4) whether any deployment/config change plausibly touched only a subset of instances (canary/rolling/partial). Return a ranked list of candidate changes with timestamps.
tasks.answer: Two changes landed within ~2 minutes of each other at the incident onset: auth-service deploy v7.3.0 at 14:00:00Z (JWT library jjwt 0.11->0.12 breaking parser API, TokenValidator rewritten) and a scheduled JWT signing-key rotation (jwt.signing.key_id k-2025-10 -> k-2026-04) at 14:01:00Z. Both are top candidates; no other service/namespace deployments or config changes occurred in the window. auth-service has no dedicated JWKS/key service in the dependency graph — it depends on user-db (postgres, platform-owned), the SHARED redis-cache, and external kyc-provider, and is called by api-gateway. tasks.objective: Correlate and disambiguate: take the onset time from task a and the candidate change/dependency list from task b and rank which change (if any) actually precedes and aligns with the onset, distinguishing a partial/canary rollout from a full one. Then search historical incidents for (i) prior invalid_token / 401 mass-logout events, (ii) prior incidents where a log-pipeline outage in one namespace masked or coincided with a real fault, and (iii) key-rotation or JWKS staleness precedents. Deliver the top hypothesis with supporting/contradicting evidence and a specific falsification test (e.g., 'if X change was rolled back at T and 401s persisted, hypothesis is dead').
tasks.answer: Ranking by (a) temporal precedence of onset and (b) alignment: the JWT signing-key rotation (jwt.signing.key_id k-2025-10 -> k-2026-04, 14:01Z, cfg-2705) is ranked #1 because onset (14:02:00) is exactly one minute after it and it is the same failure mode as precedent HIST-108 ("Key rotation published new key id before all pods loaded the JWKS"); the auth-service v7.3.0 deploy (14:00Z, dep-5710, breaking jjwt 0.11->0.12 parser rewrite) is ranked #2 — it precedes onset by 2 minutes and is a one-shot rewrite, so if it were a deterministic parser bug the plateau would be either 100% (global break) or a step matching new-instance traffic share, not a flat 36%. Neither candidate has any recorded rollback or any second change during the 14:02–15:59 plateau, so the data cannot yet separate them; the discriminating facts (per-instance version/key_id, traffic split across pods) are not exposed. The key distinction is real, not canary-vs-full: the plateau is a single discrete cliff (0.16% -> 36.08% within 60s) that never steps again, which fits a subset of pods/validators holding a stale or incompatible key/library state rather than a full-fleet break (full break would be ~100%). Falsification tests: (1) if the 401 rate is decomposed and is uniform across ALL auth-service instances/versions, the partial-state hypothesis dies; (2) if k-2026-04 was reverted (or JWKS old key re-published) and 401s persisted at 36%, the key-rotation hypothesis dies and the v7.3.0 rewrite takes #1; (3) if reverting dep-5710 (keeping the new key) does not reduce 401s, HIST-109-style library regression is dead; (4) if a non-auth caller of the JWKS/key path, or api-gateway itself, shows matching 401s, that proves a shared key/JWKS fault rather than auth-service-internal code. Precedents: invalid_token/401 mass-logout = HIST-109 and HIST-108; key-rotation/JWKS staleness = HIST-108 (re-published previous key; staged rotation). Searches for "log-pipeline outage masking a real fault" returned NO matching incident — only two unrelated dependency-failure cases (HIST-103, HIST-105), so there is no repository precedent for log-absence masking a fault.
